items.stem: In Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations model, what approximate share of adopters are 'innovators'?
items.markingKey: A. Rogers: innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34%, laggards 16%.

items.stem: Briefly explain why change caused by digital systems can be both incremental and transformative.
items.answer: Some changes are small improvements to existing practices (e.g. faster processors), while others reshape whole sectors and behaviours (e.g. smartphones transforming banking, maps and communication); the same technology can begin incrementally and become transformative as it diffuses.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Some changes are small improvements to existing practices (e.g. faster processors), while others reshape whole sectors and behaviours (e.g. smartphones transforming banking, maps and communication); the same technology can begin incrementally and become transformative as it diffuses. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The internet caused the Arab Spring." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Social media helped protesters organise and spread images, but the uprisings had deep political and economic causes (authoritarian rule, unemployment, corruption); the internet was a contributing tool, not the sole cause.
items.markingKey: Social media helped protesters organise and spread images, but the uprisings had deep political and economic causes (authoritarian rule, unemployment, corruption); the internet was a contributing tool, not the sole cause. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the next ten."
— Bill Gates, The Road Ahead (1995)

Explain what the source suggests about the pattern of technological change.
items.answer: Change often appears slow at first because adoption, infrastructure and habits take time, but cumulative diffusion produces large long-term transformations; short-term hype and long-term underestimation are both common.
items.markingKey: Change often appears slow at first because adoption, infrastructure and habits take time, but cumulative diffusion produces large long-term transformations; short-term hype and long-term underestimation are both common. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using Kodak and digital photography as an example, explain disruption by digital systems.
items.answer: Kodak dominated film photography and built an early digital camera in 1975, but protected its film business; smartphones and digital cameras eroded film sales and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012. A digital innovation from inside the firm displaced its own core product, showing how disruption can defeat even the inventor when incentives favour the old model.
items.markingKey: Context (Kodak dominated film photography and built an early digital camera in 1975, but protected its film business; smartphones and digital cameras eroded film sales and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a digital innovation from inside the firm displaced its own core product, showing how disruption can defeat even the inventor when incentives favour the old model. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to disruption by digital systems.

items.stem: "Every innovation is a disruptive innovation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most innovations are sustaining (improving existing products for existing customers); disruptive innovations specifically begin in low-end or new markets and displace incumbents.
items.markingKey: Most innovations are sustaining (improving existing products for existing customers); disruptive innovations specifically begin in low-end or new markets and displace incumbents. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using one example of disruption by a digital system, analyse the causes of the disruption and evaluate its consequences for two stakeholders.
items.answer: Choose e.g. streaming vs video rental, ride-hailing vs taxis, or e-commerce vs local retail; explain causes (cheaper technology, networks, consumer convenience, incumbents' choices); evaluate consequences for e.g. consumers and workers, using specific evidence; reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: Choose e.g. streaming vs video rental, ride-hailing vs taxis, or e-commerce vs local retail; explain causes (cheaper technology, networks, consumer convenience, incumbents' choices); evaluate consequences for e.g. consumers and workers, using specific evidence; reach a judgement.

items.stem: "Digital technologies are the main cause of social change in the 21st century." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Digital technologies are a powerful driver and amplifier of change, but they interact with social, economic and political causes; calling them the main cause overstates determinism.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smartphones and platforms have transformed work, communication and politics; the speed of diffusion (e.g. ChatGPT reaching about 100 million users within two months) is unprecedented. Arguments against: change is also driven by economics, demography, climate and politics; societies shape how technologies are adopted (social shaping); technology often amplifies existing trends rather than starting them. Supported judgement: Digital technologies are a powerful driver and amplifier of change, but they interact with social, economic and political causes; calling them the main cause overstates determinism. items.stem: Explain why disruptive innovations often succeed against established firms.
items.answer: Established firms focus on their most profitable customers and existing technology, so they ignore cheaper or simpler innovations that start in niche markets; as the innovation improves it captures mainstream customers (e.g. digital photography and Kodak).

items.stem: Distinguish between technological determinism and the social shaping of technology.
items.answer: Technological determinism holds that technology drives social change; the social shaping view argues that people, values, markets and politics shape how technologies are designed, adopted and used.

items.stem: Explain why digital platforms have increased the range of people who can express themselves publicly.
items.answer: Low-cost devices and free platforms remove traditional gatekeepers (publishers, broadcasters), so anyone with a phone can publish text, video or music to a potentially global audience.

items.stem: Explain the difference between freedom of expression and freedom of reach.
items.answer: Freedom of expression is the right to say something; "freedom of reach" refers to whether platforms amplify it – content may be allowed but demoted by algorithms.
items.markingKey: Freedom of expression is the right to say something; "freedom of reach" refers to whether platforms amplify it – content may be allowed but demoted by algorithms. items.stem: Briefly describe Iran's internet restrictions during the 2022 protests and explain what it reveals about state control of expression.
items.answer: After Mahsa Amini died in custody in September 2022, protests spread; authorities throttled mobile data and blocked Instagram and WhatsApp. The state limited the channels people used to share images and organise, showing that digital expression depends on infrastructure the state can control.
items.markingKey: Context (After Mahsa Amini died in custody in September 2022, protests spread; authorities throttled mobile data and blocked Instagram and WhatsApp.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Rafael writes: "Freedom of expression means platforms must allow any content." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Human rights law protects expression mainly against state interference and permits limits (e.g. incitement to violence); private platforms also set terms of service and must remove illegal content in many jurisdictions (e.g. under the EU DSA).
items.markingKey: Human rights law protects expression mainly against state interference and permits limits (e.g. incitement to violence); private platforms also set terms of service and must remove illegal content in many jurisdictions (e.g. under the EU DSA). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Platforms should never remove lawful content."
items.answer: Platforms need clear, transparent rules and appeal processes; a blanket ban on removing lawful content is unworkable, but removals should be proportionate and accountable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: removing lawful speech gives private firms excessive power; over-removal chills debate. Arguments against: some lawful content is harmful (harassment, self-harm promotion); platforms have rights to set community standards; lawful differs between countries. Supported judgement: Platforms need clear, transparent rules and appeal processes; a blanket ban on removing lawful content is unworkable, but removals should be proportionate and accountable.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "censorship"?
options: A culture in which people create new works by combining and modifying existing material (Lawrence Lessig, Remix, 2008)
The suppression or control of expression by governments, platforms or other powerful actors
Material such as videos, posts, reviews or fan fiction created by ordinary users rather than professional media companies
A set of free licences that let creators allow others to share and reuse their work on stated conditions, such as attribution (BY)
items.answer: The suppression or control of expression by governments, platforms or other powerful actors
items.markingKey: B. "censorship" is the suppression or control of expression by governments, platforms or other powerful actors.

items.answer: Government censorship is the state suppressing expression, often by law or blocking (e.g. internet shutdowns); platform content moderation is a private company applying its own rules to remove or limit content on its service.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers."
— Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 19 (1948)

Explain why the phrase "through any media and regardless of frontiers" is significant for digital society.
items.answer: Although written in 1948, it applies to new media such as the internet and to cross-border communication, supporting arguments against blocking, shutdowns and censorship of online platforms.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The 20th century was a read-only culture; the 21st can be read-write again, where people create by remixing the culture around them."
— Paraphrase of Lawrence Lessig, Remix (2008)

Explain what the source means by a "read-write" culture.
items.answer: A culture where people do not only consume (read) media but also create and share their own versions (write), e.g. remixes, mash-ups and memes, enabled by digital tools.
items.markingKey: A culture where people do not only consume (read) media but also create and share their own versions (write), e.g. remixes, mash-ups and memes, enabled by digital tools. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Remix culture is more creative than original creation."
items.answer: Remixing is a genuine form of creativity, but it depends on, rather than replaces, original works; balanced rules (fair use, open licences) protect both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remixing produces new meanings and lets more people create; all culture builds on earlier works. Arguments against: remixes can be low-effort copying; original creators may lose income or control; automated copyright tools limit remixing. Supported judgement: Remixing is a genuine form of creativity, but it depends on, rather than replaces, original works; balanced rules (fair use, open licences) protect both.

items.stem: Briefly explain why memes spread so quickly online.
items.answer: Memes are short, easy to copy and adapt, emotionally engaging or funny, and platforms make sharing one click; each variation reaches new networks, so they spread through participation rather than a single broadcaster.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Creative Commons licensing and copyright.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that memes have become one of the most powerful forms of political communication.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "disruptive innovation"?

The process by which an innovation spreads through a population over time, through groups from innovators to laggards (Everett Rogers, 1962)
An innovation that starts in a small or low-end market and eventually displaces established products, firms or practices (Clayton Christensen, 1997)
The ways people communicate ideas, feelings, identities and beliefs, which digital media have widened through text, images, video, sound and code

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Social media has strengthened freedom of expression more than it has threatened it."
items.answer: Social media has widened who can speak, but power over reach and visibility has shifted to platforms and states; the balance depends on context and regulation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ordinary people can publish and organise without gatekeepers (#EndSARS, #MeToo); marginalised groups gain visibility. Arguments against: surveillance and shutdowns target online speakers; harassment and pile-ons silence women and minorities; opaque moderation and algorithms decide reach. Supported judgement: Social media has widened who can speak, but power over reach and visibility has shifted to platforms and states; the balance depends on context and regulation.

items.stem: Using one example of participatory culture, analyse how it has changed the relationship between creators and audiences.
items.answer: E.g. fan fiction on AO3, TikTok duets/remixes, or Wikipedia; explain audiences becoming producers, communities setting norms, conflicts with copyright holders, and benefits/limits; reach a judgement.
items.markingKey: E.g. fan fiction on AO3, TikTok duets/remixes, or Wikipedia; explain audiences becoming producers, communities setting norms, conflicts with copyright holders, and benefits/limits; reach a judgement.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Digital technologies are the main cause of social change in the 21st century."
items.answer: Digital technologies are a powerful driver and amplifier of change, but they interact with social, economic and political causes; calling them the main cause overstates determinism.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smartphones and platforms have transformed work, communication and politics; the speed of diffusion (e.g. ChatGPT reaching about 100 million users within two months) is unprecedented. Arguments against: change is also driven by economics, demography, climate and politics; societies shape how technologies are adopted (social shaping); technology often amplifies existing trends rather than starting them. Supported judgement: Digital technologies are a powerful driver and amplifier of change, but they interact with social, economic and political causes; calling them the main cause overstates determinism. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "innovation".
items.answer: The introduction of a new or significantly improved product, process or way of doing things
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the introduction of a new or significantly improved product, process or way of doing things. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Communicating views about power, government and public issues, for example through hashtags, livestreams or online petitions"?
items.answer: political expression
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of political expression.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "user-generated content".
items.answer: Material such as videos, posts, reviews or fan fiction created by ordinary users rather than professional media companies
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: material such as videos, posts, reviews or fan fiction created by ordinary users rather than professional media companies. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is difficult to prove that a digital technology alone caused a social change.
items.answer: Social changes have multiple interacting causes – economic, political, cultural – so a technology is usually one factor among many (e.g. social media in the Arab Spring alongside unemployment, food prices and repression); correlation in time does not prove causation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Social changes have multiple interacting causes – economic, political, cultural – so a technology is usually one factor among many (e.g. social media in the Arab Spring alongside unemployment, food prices and repression); correlation in time does not prove causation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Online expression is the same as offline expression, just faster." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Online expression differs in permanence, scale, searchability and algorithmic amplification, and can be anonymous; these features change both its power and its risks.
items.markingKey: Online expression differs in permanence, scale, searchability and algorithmic amplification, and can be anonymous; these features change both its power and its risks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between viral content and a meme.
items.answer: Viral content is any content that spreads rapidly (often unchanged); a meme spreads through imitation and variation, with users creating their own versions of a format.
items.markingKey: Viral content is any content that spreads rapidly (often unchanged); a meme spreads through imitation and variation, with users creating their own versions of a format. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between transformative change and incremental change.
items.answer: Incremental change improves an existing process step by step (e.g. a faster checkout system); transformative change fundamentally alters how something is done or who does it (e.g. e-commerce reshaping retail and city centres).
items.markingKey: Incremental change improves an existing process step by step (e.g. a faster checkout system); transformative change fundamentally alters how something is done or who does it (e.g. e-commerce reshaping retail and city centres). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between freedom of reach and freedom of expression.
items.answer: Freedom of expression is the right to say something; "freedom of reach" refers to whether platforms amplify it – content may be allowed but demoted by algorithms.
items.markingKey: Freedom of expression is the right to say something; "freedom of reach" refers to whether platforms amplify it – content may be allowed but demoted by algorithms. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why participatory culture can be described as a change in the relationship between audiences and producers.
items.answer: Audiences no longer only consume media; they create, remix and distribute it (fan fiction, reaction videos), blurring the line between producer and consumer and shifting some cultural power to communities.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Audiences no longer only consume media; they create, remix and distribute it (fan fiction, reaction videos), blurring the line between producer and consumer and shifting some cultural power to communities. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the smartphone after the 2007 iPhone launch and explain what it reveals about causality and change.
items.answer: Touchscreen smartphones with app stores spread rapidly after 2007, combining camera, maps, music, banking and messaging in one device. The smartphone triggered chains of change – app economies, ride-hailing, mobile banking – but its effects also depended on cheap data plans and networks, showing multiple causes.
items.markingKey: Context (Touchscreen smartphones with app stores spread rapidly after 2007, combining camera, maps, music, banking and messaging in one device.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the smartphone triggered chains of change – app economies, ride-hailing, mobile banking – but its effects also depended on cheap data plans and networks, showing multiple causes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to causality and change.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Iran's internet restrictions during the 2022 protests shows state control of expression.
items.answer: After Mahsa Amini died in custody in September 2022, protests spread; authorities throttled mobile data and blocked Instagram and WhatsApp. The state limited the channels people used to share images and organise, showing that digital expression depends on infrastructure the state can control.
items.markingKey: Context (After Mahsa Amini died in custody in September 2022, protests spread; authorities throttled mobile data and blocked Instagram and WhatsApp.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the state limited the channels people used to share images and organise, showing that digital expression depends on infrastructure the state can control. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to state control of expression.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Anything posted online is free to remix because it is public." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Online material is usually still protected by copyright; reuse needs permission, a licence (e.g. Creative Commons) or a legal exception such as fair use/fair dealing.
items.markingKey: Online material is usually still protected by copyright; reuse needs permission, a licence (e.g. Creative Commons) or a legal exception such as fair use/fair dealing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Ice Bucket Challenge (2014) shows participatory culture.
items.answer: Participants filmed themselves pouring iced water over their heads, nominated friends and donated; the ALS Association reported about US$115 million raised. Ordinary users created and spread content themselves, turning a simple format into a global fundraising campaign through imitation and nomination.

items.stem: "The internet caused the Arab Spring." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Social media helped protesters organise and spread images, but the uprisings had deep political and economic causes (authoritarian rule, unemployment, corruption); the internet was a contributing tool, not the sole cause.

items.stem: "Remix culture is more creative than original creation." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Remixing is a genuine form of creativity, but it depends on, rather than replaces, original works; balanced rules (fair use, open licences) protect both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remixing produces new meanings and lets more people create; all culture builds on earlier works. Arguments against: remixes can be low-effort copying; original creators may lose income or control; automated copyright tools limit remixing. Supported judgement: Remixing is a genuine form of creativity, but it depends on, rather than replaces, original works; balanced rules (fair use, open licences) protect both.
